DAP token and fertilizer booking app: how to book DAP and urea online in 2026
The bag costs ₹1,350 on paper. In a shortage, the real price is a 10-hour queue and a sowing date that slips. A token cannot make more DAP, but it can stop someone else from taking yours.

Many states now sell subsidised DAP, urea and other fertilizers only against a token linked to your Farmer ID or Aadhaar and your land record. You book on the state's app or portal, or at a CSC or e-Mitra centre, choose a sale centre and date, and collect the bags within the token's time limit after OTP or thumb verification. The printed price still applies: ₹1,350 for a 50 kg bag of DAP.

Why DAP now comes with a token

India imports much of its DAP and the raw material to make it. In 2026 China, once a large supplier, has nearly stopped exporting DAP: its exports from January to July were down about 95% on the year before, and it shipped none at all in July. World prices have stayed high, so every bag is harder to bring in.

When stock is short, the queue decides who sows on time. In November 2026 farmers in Hamirpur, Uttar Pradesh waited up to 10 hours at cooperative societies and received only two bags each; in Banda, Chandauli and Prayagraj the queues and protests made the news. To stop hoarding, black marketing and fights at the counter, states are moving to tokens: the fertilizer is reserved for you against your land and crop, and you collect it on a fixed day.

How to book a fertilizer token, step by step
Get your Farmer ID made under the Farmer Registry if you do not have one. A CSC or your agriculture office can do it.
Install the official app named in your state, or visit a CSC or e-Mitra centre.
Log in with your Farmer ID or Aadhaar. An OTP comes to your Aadhaar-linked mobile.
Check that your land shows correctly: survey, khasra or khata number and area.
Choose this season's crop and the area you will sow. The app shows how many bags you can book.
Pick the sale centre and the date, and submit. Save the booking ID or token as a screenshot.
Go on that date, within the token's time limit, with Aadhaar. Verify by OTP or thumb.
Pay the printed price and take a bill.
Documents to keep ready
Aadhaar card, and the mobile number linked to it.
Farmer ID, where your state has started the Farmer Registry.
Land record: 7/12, khatauni or the state's record, with survey or khasra number and area.
Tenants and sharecroppers: the lease paper or the self-declaration your state asks for.
Money for the printed price, in cash or UPI as the centre accepts.
Common problems and what to do
Token booked but no stock at the centre: ask the society when the next rake is due and book again for that date.
Token expired: in Rajasthan a token lasts 48 hours. Book again.
Land not showing: your land record or Farmer ID needs updating. Go to the CSC or the patwari or talati.
OTP not coming: your mobile is not linked to Aadhaar, or the number has changed. Update it at an Aadhaar centre.
Dealer asks more than ₹1,350 for DAP, or forces you to buy another product with it: refuse, ask for a bill, and complain to your district agriculture office.
Beware of fake apps and fake DAP
Download only the official app, published by the government department. Do not install apps sent as links on WhatsApp.
No real token system asks you to pay an advance to a person or a UPI ID.
Check every bag: printed price, company name, batch number and date. Buy only with a bill.
Very cheap DAP sold door to door is a warning sign.

A cumin farmer near Rajkot put no DAP in his field. At 60 days, his neighbours said they had never seen cumin like it. He had not found a secret bag. He had stopped feeding only the crop and started feeding the soil.

Farmers in Gujarat have grown cumin with no DAP at all and sugarcane on half their usual chemical fertilizer, using Immunity Granules in the soil, the Immunity Special for their crop and Immunity Gold. These are their own field experiences, not a promise. The approach works best on old farms, where years of DAP have left phosphorus locked in the soil.

Why many farms can do without DAP for a season

Only about 15 to 25% of the phosphorus in fertilizer becomes available to the crop. The rest stays in the soil, locked with calcium in alkaline soils or with iron and aluminium in acid soils. After 20 or 30 years of DAP, most old farms hold a large bank of this phosphorus.

So the real question is not only where to buy the next bag. It is how to get the crop's roots to the phosphorus you have already paid for. That needs a loose, living soil and a big, healthy root system. This is what the Immunity program is made for. The science is explained in how to free locked phosphorus.
Bharatbhai, cumin, Lariya village, Padadhari (Rajkot): no DAP at all
Bharatbhai has grown cumin for 30 to 35 years. This season he used Immunity Granules at sowing, Immunity Cumin Special through the irrigation water, and sprays of Immunity Gold with Cumin Special.

In front of our team and his neighbours he said he had put no DAP in the field. He gave urea only once, a small amount, and mainly to carry a fungicide. At 60 days his cumin was even and green, with more than 95% of the plants standing, and in full flower.

He said that in 30 to 35 years he had seen cumin like this only once: this season. He expected about 13 to 14 man per bigha (20 kg to a man). A farmer from the next village, looking at the field, estimated his own cumin at about 4 to 5 man. Bharatbhai also said his cost was lower than with full chemical fertilizer. These were his estimates at 60 days, in his own words.
Budhabhai Patel, sugarcane: half the bags of chemical fertilizer

Budhabhai planted variety 86032 on 3 September with Immunity Granules, Immunity Sugarcane Special and Immunity Gold. The plot next to his, planted two or three days apart, got 10 to 12 bags of chemical fertilizer. His got 6.
He counted 8 to 12 tillers per clump, and said he expected nearly all of them to reach the mill rather than die in the shade.
Falguniben Patel, sugarcane, Nani Chovisi (Navsari): less urea, green leaves at harvest

Falguniben planted 86002 in October 2025 and the mill's first cutting began on 24 October 2026. She used Immunity Granules, Immunity Sugarcane Special and Immunity Gold with our schedule, and kept urea at about 2 to 2.5 bags where farmers might otherwise use 3 or 4.

At cutting the leaves were still green and the canes long, and she said her cost was a little lower than in earlier years, when rising chemical prices pushed it up. She said she would recommend the products to other farmers.
Jitendrabhai Patel, castor, Vadnagar (Mehsana): roots deep in hard soil

Jitendrabhai applied Immunity Granules in pits in his 6 vigha of castor (variety Avni 11). His soil is hard, and he said the roots went deep, the plants stayed dark green, and fungus was lower than in his other castor field. He has since used the granules in tobacco and plans to use them in wheat.

Locked phosphorus: how to free the DAP you have already paid for
Every bag of DAP you ever bought is partly still in your field. It did not wash away. It turned into calcium phosphate, a rock the roots cannot eat, waiting for something to dissolve it.

Only about 15-25% of the phosphorus you apply as fertilizer becomes available to the crop. The rest is locked by calcium in alkaline soils, or by iron and aluminium in acid soils, and builds up over the years. Humic substances, phosphate-solubilising microbes, organic matter, a looser soil with deeper roots, and products placed in the root zone by drench or drip help the crop reach it.

higher wheat yield with humic acids in one alkaline-soil study
Where your DAP goes

India's National Academy of Agricultural Sciences reports that only 15 to 25% of fertilizer phosphorus becomes available to plants, and only 1 to 3% of all the phosphorus in a soil is available at any time. In alkaline soils, above pH 7, phosphorus reacts with calcium and magnesium. In acid soils, below pH 6, it reacts with iron and aluminium. Either way it turns into forms that roots cannot easily take up.

Much of Gujarat has alkaline, calcium-rich black and coastal soils. Here a large share of each DAP bag ends up as calcium phosphate. It is not lost; it is locked. And after decades of DAP, many fields hold a large bank of it.
Signs your soil is holding phosphorus back
The soil test shows medium or high phosphorus, but the crop still shows phosphorus hunger: slow early growth, weak roots, a purple tinge on young wheat or maize leaves.
Yields have stopped rising though you use more DAP every year.
The soil is hard and crusts after irrigation, and water stands on the surface.
Fields fed DAP for years run short of zinc. See zinc and phosphorus.
Five ways to bring locked phosphorus back

Humic substances. In a study on alkaline soil (Wang and others, Soil Use and Management, 1995), adding humic acids with phosphorus fertilizer increased water-soluble phosphate, slowed the formation of locked forms, and raised phosphorus uptake and wheat yield by 25%. See humic acid and the root zone.

Microbes that dissolve phosphate. Phosphate-solubilising bacteria and fungi release organic acids that dissolve calcium phosphate near the roots. The national academy recommends such consortia, with mycorrhiza, to raise phosphorus use. See Immunity PSB, PSF and Mycorrhiza.
Organic matter. Compost and well-rotted farmyard manure release phosphorus slowly and keep it in forms roots can use. See compost and humic acid.
Bigger roots. Phosphorus barely moves, so the roots must come to it. A larger, deeper root system, extended by mycorrhiza, reaches far more of the soil.
Placement. Phosphorus and products placed near the seed or in the root zone work better than the same amount spread on top.
A softer soil, deeper roots

Hard, compact soil keeps roots short and shallow, so they touch only a thin layer of the phosphorus bank. When soil life and organic matter return, the soil crumbles, holds air and water, and roots travel deeper.

A living soil also holds nutrients better. Soil scientists call this the cation exchange capacity: the soil's power to hold calcium, magnesium, potash and other nutrients like a sponge and release them to the roots. Organic matter raises it. And around every active root, the acids made by roots and microbes lower the pH in a thin zone, where locked calcium phosphate dissolves even when the rest of the soil stays alkaline.

Immunity Granules are made for exactly this: hard, compact soil, weak soil life and poor roots. The crop's Immunity Special, given with irrigation water or through drip, goes straight into that root zone. Jitendrabhai of Vadnagar saw his castor roots go deep into hard soil after using the granules.

Why does my crop show phosphorus deficiency even after DAP?

Most of the DAP phosphorus gets locked in the soil, by calcium in alkaline soils or iron and aluminium in acid soils. Hard soil and weak roots make it worse. The crop needs a living soil and strong roots to reach it.
Can I free phosphorus without adding more DAP?
Yes, partly. Humic substances, phosphate-solubilising microbes, organic matter, deeper roots and placing products in the root zone all help the crop use phosphorus already in the soil.
Does humic acid release phosphorus?
Studies on alkaline soils show humic acids keep more phosphate soluble and slow its locking, so the crop takes up more.
Is high pH soil bad for phosphorus?
Above pH 7, phosphorus reacts with calcium and gets locked. Roots and microbes can dissolve it again in the zone right around the root.
How long do PSB take to work?
They start working once the soil is moist and warm, and work best with organic matter. The benefit builds over the season and over seasons.

Urea and potash shortage: how humic acid, seaweed and amino acids help you need fewer bags
Of every three bags of urea, more than one may never reach the crop. When urea and potash are short, the cheapest bag is the one you stop losing.

Indian crops use only about 30-45% of the nitrogen in urea; the rest is lost to the air and to leaching. You can need fewer bags by splitting urea, placing it well and using biostimulants and microbes: humic acid keeps nutrients in the root zone, seaweed extract and amino acids help the plant use what it takes up and cope with stress, and bacteria add nitrogen and free potash. Many farmers have cut urea this way; it does not mean starving the crop.
nitrogen use efficiency of urea in India
nitrogen in urea: no organic bag matches it, so cut the losses
Where your urea goes

In India, heavy urea use has pulled nitrogen use efficiency down to about 30 to 45%. Most of the rest escapes as gas from urea left on the soil surface, or washes below the roots with irrigation water. Too much urea also makes crops soft and lush, so pests and diseases come faster and the crop can fall over.
So every bag saved from loss is a bag you do not need to buy. When urea, DAP or potash is short, that matters twice.
Use fewer bags of urea
Split urea into two or three doses at the stages the crop needs it, instead of one heavy dose.
Give it just before irrigation, or mix it into the soil. Urea left on dry, hot soil turns to gas.
Do not overdo early doses. Watch the leaf colour, and add more only if the crop turns pale.
Use nitrogen-fixing bacteria: Azotobacter for wheat and vegetables, Azospirillum for cereals, Acetobacter for sugarcane and Rhizobium for pulses.
Return crop residues and add compost. Organic matter releases nitrogen slowly through the season.
Potash: the bag many farmers skip, and how to stretch it
Potash fills grain, tubers, fruit and sugar, and helps the crop stand heat, cold and disease.
Many Indian soils hold potash locked in their minerals. Potash-mobilising bacteria such as Immunity KMB help release it.
Crop residues are rich in potash. Burning them or carrying them away takes that potash off the farm.
Do not skip potash for potato, banana or sugarcane on soils that test low.

What is the organic alternative to urea?

No organic product carries 46% nitrogen. What works is cutting losses and adding biological nitrogen: split urea, nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Azotobacter, Azospirillum, Acetobacter and Rhizobium, compost, and biostimulants that help the crop use nitrogen better.
Can I stop urea completely?
Pulses can need little or none when Rhizobium is active. For most other crops, reduce urea step by step and watch the crop, rather than stopping at once.
What can replace potash?
Potash-mobilising bacteria release potash locked in soil minerals, and returning crop residues brings potash back. On soils that test low, potato, banana and sugarcane still need potash fertilizer.
Do seaweed and humic acid reduce fertilizer need?
They help the crop take up and use nutrients better and cope with stress, so many farmers can use fewer bags. They work alongside good nutrition, not in place of all of it.
How do I know I have cut too much nitrogen?
Older leaves turn pale yellow first and growth slows. Give a split dose of urea and adjust next time.
